question.prompt:
In the figure below, \(3\) of the \(6\) disks are to be painted blue, \(2\) are to be painted red, and \(1\) is to be painted green. Two paintings that can be obtained from one another by a rotation or a reflection of the entire figure are considered the same. How many different paintings are possible?

[Figure 1](figures/2017_AMC_10B_Q18_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The single green disk gives us a way to orient each painting before counting. In the triangular arrangement, the three corner positions can be rotated into one another, as can the three positions between corners. A corner position cannot be moved to a position between corners by a symmetry of the figure.

There are therefore two cases: green at a corner, or green between corners. In the first case, rotate green to the top disk. In the second, rotate green to the bottom middle disk. In either case, the only remaining symmetry besides leaving everything in place is reflection across the vertical line through green.

With green fixed, choose two of the other five disks to be red; the remaining three must be blue. There are
\[
\frac{5\cdot4}{2}=10
\]
red-position choices, where division by \(2\) removes the two orders of choosing the same pair.

The vertical reflection fixes one of these five positions and exchanges the other four in two mirror pairs. A red choice is unchanged by reflection exactly when the two red disks form one complete mirror pair. Thus exactly two choices are unchanged. The other eight choices form four pairs of different reflected paintings, so each green-position case contributes
\[
2+\frac{8}{2}=6
\]
different paintings.

Every painting belongs to one of the two green-position cases. Within either case, the reflection accounts for all possible identifications, and the two cases cannot overlap. Therefore the total is \(2\cdot6=\boxed{12}\), choice D.
solutions.title: Fix the green disk
